As part of his engagement with technology, the later Heidegger developed a rich notion of dwelling. Dwelling as he uses it entails an ecological attunement to the environment, although it will mean more than this. It differs from, say, the idea that we all have worldviews, which would make dwelling a matter of properly tempering our cultural knowledge. Worldviews, as I have argued, posit a more or less stable common reality variously shaping or shaped by human culture and language. The notion of worldviews invokes the subjective, writ large as society, and thereby gives over to (Western) science the authority to pronounce the truth of nature. A worldview thus constitutes how the world appears "out theren as colored by cultural lenses, a position that insinuates a disengagement between people and world, so that ultimately "objective" reason becomes the means to eliminate cultural distortion and get at the actual essence of things (Ingold 15). 2 As Heidegger argues, however, dwelling indicates not a worldview but a principle of being: culture is materially enworlded. That is, dwelling is a way of being conditioned and permeated by things so that they are inseparable from what it means to live in the world. But dwelling also has a hermeneutic character, in that, like Dasein, questions

of being are continually at issue (see Heidegger, BT 32). The question of how existence is best pursued is not simply given as knowledge but achieved through continual questioning. Such questioning and formulating does not reside solely with the human. Thus, dwelling is not mere survival or existence, nor is it the layering of culture over mundane reality. Dwelling is characterized by thriving or "flourishing" conceived in an ecological key (Heidegger, DT 47). It is not simply an ensemble of practices or habits whose daily performance gets marked by the style we then associate with a particular community. Rather, dwelling indicates lived relations woven into complex ecologies of the world's things and forces. This is not passive coexistence or simple adaptation to things; it is an active if conditioned comportment toward the world. Indeed, this is why Heidegger connects dwelling with building (PLT 146, 148).3By doing so, he grounds human flourishing in constructive activity. That is, the attunement to the world that characterizes dwelling is not passivity. Rather, it is activity that works through and with things as they show up in the world alongside us. Heidegger characterizes this relationship as a dynamic kind of''letting ben appearing as forms of shepherding, cultivating, sparing, and ca retaking (PLT 147-48).

Heidegger's terminology is overly rustic, an important and not unproblematic consideration. Heidegger incorporated such attitudes into much of his thought. When he turned to technological artifacts in his critical ruminations on technology, he often found them to lack a special status he reserved for "things," which were as often as not illustrated through rustic examples. A wine jug is a thing, but a river dam is an object, and in the later Heidegger, the "object" label conveys a negative valuation. I think we must resist this valuation but not simply reject it. Rather, we might ask what stakes lie in making a distinction between a thing and an object. Can this distinction tells us anything that bears on rhetoric and its relation to things and how we dwell with them, even as we move past the limitations we recognize in Heidegger's particular articulation of this distinction? These questions indicate that Heidegger's romanticizations are more than evocations of the rustic. In order to explain this, I want to look at what Heidegger has to say about things and, in particular, how he wants to grant to the thing, as opposed to the object, the ability to manifest what he calls the fourfold (das Geviert). The fourfold is the gathering of earth, sky, mortals, and gods-admittedly a rather oblique statement. Because the Timaeus deals pervasively with the question of beginnings, it is appropriate to see it also as a recommencement of the task that was central to the Republic, which is to bring Athens back to its ideal form (at the time of the dialogue, apparently, the interlocutors saw it as less than it had been). What we learn from the Republic is that while the ideal city they describe evokes powerful feelings and approval, it remains an ideal. It misses actuality, and the discussants hope this condition is rectifiable, that this city ideal can be brought to life and seen vigorously exercising as states do (Timaeus 18b). As it is, the ideal city is a dead city. Sallis remarks that, strictly speaking, it is a "technical city," a city of the head achieved through philosophical technique (20). Not only is it a fabricated artifact of thought, but it lacks eros, which is to say, it lacks becoming in a generative sense. The fact that the Republic focuses strongly on controlling eros and all that goes with it, such as "procreation, mating, birth, sexual difference, [and] corporeity itself in its singularity," takes on greater significance in this context (Sallis 26). There is thus a tension between control as something intellectual and life as something that exceeds the intellectual. For this reason, among others, Sallis tells us that from the very beginning, the Timaeus comments on the limits of fabrication, whether as techne or poiesis, with respect to eros (26). This is very much a problem of invention in the sense of finding ways to actualize or enact what are initially only ideas, feelings, or intuitions. That is, the Platonic chora addresses the question of the available means of creation and how we give life to and make a place for (static) ideas. Furthermore, the discussion implicitly evokes a distinction

between the made and the born, or between techni and physis. The chora gains even greater import when we see that it emerges precisely to dissolve such distinctions and give life to artifice.

Friedrich Solmsen argues that we can understand Plato to be wrestling with a problem that reaches far back into debates carried on by the pre-Socratics. How is one to understand genesis, or becoming? Parmenides is held to have dismissed any outright genesis; Empedocles refined Parmenides's thought, suggesting instead that something akin t omixture, achieved through the interactions of the four elements or roots (see chapter 7), could replace genesis. The Timaeus itself addresses this issue, but it does so as a reopening of the question of becoming. Throughout the dialogue, the uncertainty of knowing anything about genesis is remarked, and even the accounts given are characterized as only probable or likely (Timaeus 28b, 44d, 48c-d, 55d, 59c. 66d). ln this regard, the ch6ra can be taken as Plato's attempt to reintroduce the notion of becoming, even ifhe steps back from the more assertive positions of his predecessors (Solmsen 40). At the risk of oversimplifying, we might say that Plato posited this refined notion of genesis as an aid in thinking through how, as Algra puts it, the sensible world participates in the intelligible world (3). Ann Ashbaugh makes a similar point when she claims that the Timaeus was the mast important Platonic dialogue in antiquity because it addressed a fundamental question, one that we have yet to answer definitively: not "what an objective cosmos is, but how it comes to be known by the souln (1). Apropos ofSallis's comment on the limits of fabrication, the Republic already carries in germinal form this very question: haw does one move from ideas, or the realm of the Forms. to the sensible, active world?

This sensible, active world is not one of simple presence or mundane materiality. The Greeks, like other ancient peoples, had a strong sense of what remains hidden, obscure, and withdrawn in the world. Indeed. the ancient sense of the divine was itself tethered to place, as E. V. Walter argues throughout his book Placeways. Empedocles and Heidegger continually emphasized the need to forge a positive way forward, to work not just with who people are but with where they are. We cannot escape the infrastructures, industries, and lifeways people currently have but must work within and through them towards a more ecologically attuned dwelling. In this regard, science, technology, and capitalism will need to become part of that path, despite the fact that these are some of the most common targets for environmentalist critique. On these points I take inspiration from Peter Sloterdijk's digression on spaceships in his massive philosophical trilogy, Spheres. Sloterdijk argues that spaceships are more than technological objects—they are equally ontological interventions. The suturing

of a thing to ontology harkens back to Heidegger, and we can see how Sloterdijk's spaceship updates Heidegger's jugs and bridges. But there is also an inversion: jugs and bridges evoke an interconnected whole to which we are all wedded and indebted; a spaceship, however, operates in a realm of extreme inhospitality. Space is nonconductive for nearly all life as we know it. Since no aspect of dwelling in space can be taken for granted, a spaceship "constitutes a world model," a kind of "immanence machine."73 The level of explicatory detail necessary for surviving in such a harsh environment is vertiginous. To give one small example: astronauts must sleep with fans next to them, less their exhalations, which do not move in zero gravity, suffocate them in a bubble of nitrogen and carbon dioxide.74 There is no resting on unexplicated assumptions, as is possible back on Earth where the ecological background can simply be assumed, as Moore exemplifed through capitalism's cavalier appropriations of nature. Space lacks such "ontological comfort."75

The point, Sloterdijk argues, is that "space travel amounts to an ontological alphabetization: what follows from it is that the elements of being-in-the-world can, and must, be written."76 Sloterdijk picks up the thread we saw connecting Empedocles and Aristotle in the movement from roots to elements, where increasing abstraction and alphabetization formalize as science and episteme. Sloterdijk also counters Abram's argument that abstraction goes hand in hand with the West's loss of intimacy with the environment. Rather, Sloterdijk taps a great affrmation resonant with Empedocles and Heidegger. It is the affrmation of the fourfold. The lesson is that abstraction and alphabetization also gather the fourfold and disclose the worldly depths of rich interconnection. Spaceships necessitate this insight. For life to maintain itself in space, bubbles of lifeworld must be constructed. To construct a bubble of lifeworld requires a profoundly rich explication of an ecological background we take for granted on earth, where our lifeworld is simply given. For spacecraft, these ABCs of lifeworlding must be spelled out and implemented through the technics of disclosure and building. As Heidegger has argued, to build is to dwell, and here we see how this manifests in even the most focused technological enterprise.77

The explicative disclosure necessary for space travel thus affrms some of environmentalism's biggest demons—abstraction, science, technology, capitalist progress. But this disclosive work pushes through their dangers and lights up their roles in the ecological lifeworld it is claimed they despoil. Still, it may be argued that space travel is a feeting pursuit

Here the line between the Rhetorical and the Symbolic falls away. Such is likewise the case when a Rhetorical pose is, in a deeper sense, genuine (as with Oscar Wilde, who insisted upon the genuineness of the poseur, doubtless in his awareness that with him literary perversity was a true counterpart of sexual perversion). Psychotic “malingering” likewise falls in this indeterminate area, as the person who feigns illness for pur­ poses of evasion really and truly is the sort of person who feigns illness for purposes of evasion. The Gidean “esthetic criminal” (who commits crime not for advan­ tage but for love of the art, as self-portraiture) responds to a kind of epideictic motive insofar as a poetic love of plot here finds expression in a cult of the plotter, or a love of design in a cult of the designing. But such rhetorical “freedom” is quite the same as Symbolic “necessity,” since the deliberate choice to “be oneself” under such conditions is like­ wise a compulsion. A Rhetoric of advantage enters, insofar as the artifi­ cer’s gestures are claims to distinction, however uncomfortable and even sacrificial. For they can be insignia proclaiming proud enrollment in a very noble but sinister heraldic line, ancestral blood that nurtures the strong stock of bastardy. (Cf. Gide’s tributes to the fils naturel, whom he admires, we might say, as a source of bright new private enterprise.) Character itself can, in turn, be considered in two ways: (1) one’s identity as an individual (who rounds out his nature by acts in keeping with it); (2) one’s identity as member of a class, in a particular position or social status, etc. Often those who treat “ritual” motives as primary in human conduct have in mind some such relations between agent and act whereby the agent “expresses himself in his conduct” (or, we might say, adopts such actions as “imitate” his nature or are “analogous with” it).
